Sir John Willison, for weeks and months, carried the slogan across the page of that newspaper, "Concessions for Concessions," representing the maximum rates proposed in the Crowsnest pass contract as then, in 1897, and forever applicable to shipments from every point on the Canadian Pacific system in Canada. Ontario and British Columbia Liberalism, however, generally resisted the cor-porationizing of their party. Sir William Mulock and Mr. J. F. Lister would have beaten the Crowsnest pass proposals to death if parliament had ever understood that the Canadian Pacific Railway had the right to apply Crowsnest rates to shipments from certain points while refusing those rates to shipments from other points.
Now, what is the use of the Supreme Court of Canada and the Board of Railway Commissioners writing into the contract something that was never in the minds of the parties to that contract, something that was altogether foreign to the original intention? I have here extracts from speeches delivered in parliament in 1897, and while I will not weary the committee by reading them, I may mention for the information of hon. members the pages of Hansard of that year at which the views of these several gentlemen may be found. For example, at page 5347 of Hansard of 1S97 the Minister of Railways and Canals of that day, the late Mr. Blair, expresses himself in strong terms in relation to the agreement. At page 4581 of Hansard of the same year Mr. Mclnnes said in regard to the concessions:
But even if they were of enormous nominal value, you will admit that they are, so far, mere paper concessions and that the real value of them will depend on their administration.
But although he qualified himself to that extent he did not think that the deal was at all advisable. He was opposed to it. At page 5182 Mr. Wallace declared that in his opinion that part of the bargain providing that the Crowsnest pass railway should come under the General Railway Act was not worth five cents to the country; nor, in his opinion, were the concessions given by the Canadian Pacific Railway. Again, at page 5344 of Hansard of the same year, we have the views of Mr. Lister on the subject.
Time will not permit me to quote the opinions of these gentlemen, but hon. members will find them interesting reading. Now, if the Mulock Liberals and the Lister Liberals had defeated the Crowsnest pass deal they would have saved this country, it is estimated, some $400,000,000. The surrender to the Canadian Pacific Railway in the Crowsnest pass fight was the beginning of this country's railway misfortunes. These mistakes and follies were the source of all Canada's railway troubles, and the cash cost of these troubles now totals nearly $500,000,000. The $55,000,000 deficit on the year's operations of the Canadian National Railways had its origin in the Crowsnest pass iniquity and is a yearly burden which we can attribute primarily to that source. The directorate of the Canadian Pacific Railway have conceived and disseminated this propaganda of "the iniquity of discrimination" as a means of empowering that company to repudiate the Crowsnest pass contract. In my opinion Canada's railway commission should have abolished this discrimination by deciding that the Crowsnest rates should stand; they could have abolished the discrimination by the simple expedient of maintaining the Crowsnest pass contract. But Canada's railway commission chose to bring about this end by the appalling decision that authorized the friends of the Canadian Pacific Railway, as the Soviet government does in similar circumstances, to repudiate its contracts. Why should the Canadian Pacific Railway be permitted to keep the Crowsnest pass cash and coal land subsidies as well as other valuable considerations which they received, while they are allowed to disregard entirely the agreement by means of which they secured these considerations? A Crowsnest pass contract that is no longer a contract but merely a scrap of paper, as regards reduced freight rates which the Canadian Pacific covenanted to give, should certainly not be considered a contract in regard to the enormous subsidy which this country not only undertook to deliver but actually did deliver to that company. I would make the Canadian Pacific Railway carry out its contract. I believe if part of the Crowsnest pass contract is scrapped as now in this act, the whole of it should be scrapped, and the Canadian Pacific Railway should be taken into the Exchequer court and forced to give back all the subsidies and other valuable considerations and privileges which it received under the contract from the government of Canada and the government of Manitoba.
With all respect to the railway commission, I regret to say, Mr. Chairman, that it has no
Railway Freight Rates

longer the confidence of the people of Canada. The municipalities of Ontario in the past few years have had about a dozen cases before the board regarding telephone, express, freight and passenger rates, and in every case the board accepted the figures submitted by the public service corporations and granted their applications for increased rates. In fact, the railway commission is really a political commission, for its orders are subject to appeal to and revision by the Governor in Council, and in that way its activities are not removed from the realm of polities. On the contrary, the Interstate Commerce Commission in the United States is absolutely free from political interference and its decisions are based on economic principles and are just and equitable. According to the Kailway Act the Board of Railway Commissioners are supposed to deal with rates of their own volition on the principle of equality of treatment for the whole Dominion, but the board has never been known of its own volition and for the protection of the public to go out and fight and check up freight, telephone, express and passenger rates from coast to coast. In my opinion the railway commission should be reconstituted, reorganized and placed then in a position to deal with the adjustment of rates absolutely without any right of appeal from its decisions to the Privy Council of Canada. Then it would be able to determine these matters, not on sectional but on national lines, basing every decision on the principle of equality of treatment. If we had had chief commissioners like the late Mr. Justice Mabee and the ablest chairman the board ever had, the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), we would not have these troubles to-day. They never fixed rates that were not just and equitable to everybody concerned and they had public confidence. In 1909 the Bell Telephone Company were charging $80 to $100 per telephone per annum in the Deer Park district, while just across the road where their regular tolls were in effect the rate was $32. We took the case to the railway commission, and Mr. Justice Mabee wielded the big stick on the telephone company. He said that it did not cost a consumer any more for his electric light, his water, or his gas because he was further away from the source of suppiy than some of his neighbours, and the same principle should be applied with respect to the telephone. So he brought to time that company which had been paying eight per cent for thirty-two years and ordained a flat rate for the whole city of $32. If we had more men of the type of the late Mr. Justice Mabee and his successor the

hon. member for West York, the municipalities would have more confidence in the commission. They never fixed rates on any sectional principle, but always on the principle of equality and justice and fair dealing, and therefore their decisions were always just and equitable.
It is all very well for the government to give eastbound grain and flour the benefit of the Crowsnest pass agreement, but what about other sections of the country and their products? The people in eastern and central Canada will have to pay for the piece-meal abrogation of the Crowsnest pass agreement. All along the railway commission has failed to protect central Canada. The east paid the biggest part of the cost of constructing western lines, and it should not be discriminated against by such class legislation as this. The railway commission should do its part or be removed; it should see that any order it issues does not rob Peter to pay Paul, as has been the practice in the past. It is unfortunate that while we are united in many ways, owing to our rate structure being built largely on sectional and political lines, on transportation matters we are rent asunder instead of working together for the good of the Dominion. I sympathize with British Columbia, with the prairie provinces and with the Maritime provinces, but while they are contemplating their various ills, I would ask them not to forget old central Canada which has borne the heaviest burden of the national debt, which is paying the largest proportion of the taxes and does not object to continue doing so, but simply asks for just treatment-fair rates based on economic and not sectional principles and, in short, a square deal all round- equal rights to all, special privileges to none.

Mr. Chairman, at
this late stage of the debate one can hardly hope to exercise much influence on the government or the House, for presumably the government at last has made up its mind in regard to this question. Our railway problem is to my mind the greatest that we have to face in Canada to-day. So much depends upon transportation that anything that can be done to free the people from inequality of freight rates should merit the careful consideration and approval of the government. I believe that our burdens of taxation and railway costs of transportation are crushing industry to the ground, and are responsible for many of our natural resources remaining dormant and undeveloped. The mad, drunken spree of railway construction extravagance that this country indulged in a few decades ago appeared to be a nightmare to many of

Railway Freight Rates
us for a long time, but we are beginning to realize that it is a very uncomfortable reality, and we are now paying the price. The consequences of that folly cannot be evaded. The railway problem must be faced by the people as a national unit, rather than in a selfish sectional spirit, one section endeavouring to obtain an advantage regardless of its effect on the other parts of the Dominion. From the expressions of opinion which we have had on this bill, it is absolutely hopeless to expect freight rates to be satisfactorily adjusted by parliament. I believe that the Board of Railway Commissioners is the proper tribunal to deal with this matter. Iif that board is not properly constituted to deal with the problem then men with a thorough training and experience along these lines should be appointed to that body. I am not criticizing the present board, but I do contend that the railway commission is the proper body to adjust railway rates. There is such a great need for expert knowledge in connection with this question that it is absolutely hopeless for a member of this House, with his other duties, to become seized of the facts and arrive at a proper decision as to what the scale of rates should be. I am at a loss to understand, in view of the old Crowsnest pass agreement which has been a disturbing factor in this country for many years, why the government do not give the railway commission absolute power to deal with this question. Why have they obtruded this phase of the matter in such a way as to tie the hands of the commission, and prevent an adjustment of rates that would result in an equality in all parts of the Dominion? Hon. gentlemen to my left are apparently very suspicious that western Canada would suffer as a result. Well, if that is the opinion of people in some provinces what is the use of having a railway commission at all? What is the use of such a board if we are not going to place confidence in it, if we are not going to give it full power to deal with this matter? Everyone admits that it is impossible for us to handle the situation as it should be handled in parliament. Apparently the government, have no views on the question themselves. In the session of 1922, on May 4, they appointed a select committee to deal with the question of the Crowsnest pass rates and to report to parliament. We also had last night the views of an ex-minister of the present government (Mr. McMurray), a gentleman who resigned from the cabinet a few weeks ago, and he informed the House that it was always the intention of the government to have the Crowsnest pass rates go into effect
again. I have heard no satisfactory explanation-an fact I have heard no explanation at all-as to why the government are going to introduce this fragment of the Crowsnest pass agreement into the railway rates structure. The Prime Minister waxed eloquent shortly before the House rose at one o'clock as to the government's desire to have equality of rates in Canada, and yet we have the most positive evidence in this legislation that the government do not propose or intend to allow anything of the kind. On- the contrary the bill we are now considering will render it impossible for the railway commission to do its duty as it was supposed to be anxious to do.
The conditions in Canada to-day are not the same as they were when this agreement went into effect; they are entirely different from the conditions which prevailed at that time. The Crowsnest pass agreement is something that the people of this country knew little or nothing about until the last few years. It was one of the first acts of a new government in 1897. They tried their prentice hands on railway legislation and the Crowsnest pass agreement was the product of their efforts. It remained in abeyance for a long time. In 1903 legislation was passed creating the Board of Railway Commissioners, and they have been administering the railway rates, and questions arising in connection therewith ever since. But during the war time there was another condition which has apparently been overlooked, but which was referred to by the chairman of the railway commission in 1921 when the board made a thorough inspection of railway conditions in western Canada. I should like to direct the attention of hon. gentlemen to some of the remarks made by the chairman of that body at that time. They will be found in the Canadian Annual Review for 1921. I quote from that publication as follows:
The railway board visited the western centres in the spring of 1921, and heard various appeals and statements as to freight rates; outside of the commission sittings, Mr. Carvell continued >his outspoken utterances. [DOT]Speaking to the Canadian Club at Brandon on April 22, lie described the railway problem as more important than the tariff or any other question before the people.
I quite agree with him. I believe that railway transportation is the most important question in this country at the present time. He went on to say:
It cost $40,000,000 more to run the Canadian National railways last year than was brought in and that is no reflection on the people at the head of the railways or on the government.
I quote a little further on from this publication as follows:
Railway Freight Rates

At Victoria (April 11) he told the Canadian Club that freight rates on Canadian railways were too high; that in many cases they were having an adverse effect upon business; that under existing circumstances and the McAdoo and Chicago wage awards this could not be helped; that to force the railways to meet increased costs of operation without the privilege of raising rates or power of lowering wages would be to force the roads against the wall; that the financial stability of the Canadian Pacific Railway was as important to the country as good government. He declared that the root of the trouble was in payrolls forced upon this country by political agitation and labour efforts in the United States; that "the action of American labour men in putting a pistol to the head of the Canadian railway companies and demanding that the new American wage scale, fixed under the Chicago award, be male effective in Canada, placed the railway companies in a most humiliating position".
As to the future: "no matter what happens, railway labour must be re-born and an honest day's labour for an honest day's pay must be the first principle observed. Canadian labour is not responsible for the McAdoo award, but it is responsible if it is not prepared to give honest service."
Let me quote further;
His view of the labour situation was important because it could not but affect the policy and decisions of tlhe board: "there are engineers and conductors today who are making 54,000, $5,000, and even $6,000 a year as the result of the McAdoo award; I am beginning to be sceptical of the advisability of having Canadian unions controlled in the United States.
Dealing with this question in the Canadian House of Commons in the session of 1920 the Minister of Railways of that time referred to the affect of the McAdoo and Chicago awards which had been forced upon the government, and pointed out;
The wage bill for the year exceeded seventy-three millions, having, owing largely to the McAdoo series of advances, jumped from fifty-four millions in 1918. In other words, out of every one dollar of revenue you earn, seventy-eight cents passed directly, by way of wages, to the employees.
Now, these are conditions that did not exist when the Crowsnest pass agreement went into effect and we might as well realize that now as any other time, and why the government want to interject part of the old Crowsnest pass agreement into this legislation under present conditions is beyond my understanding. The rates in the bill in question are the rates on grain and flour, not rates on the by-products, not the rates on live stock; there is no inducement offered to the people in the district affected to convert the products of the farm into a finished product and ship it out in that way. No preference of that kind :s given now on mill feed. The policy of the government seems to be:	Ship out the raw
material in as crude a state as possible; exploit the resources of the country. Every inducement is being offered along these lines. If it is the intention of the government to afford aid to facilitate the production of these commodities why not adopt some other means. 
and leave it out of the Railway Act altogether? If it is a form of protection that is going to be adopted for certain classes in certain sections, let us frankly admit it, but keep it out of the railway rates structure, and allow the railway commission to adopt a rate schedule that will apply without prejudice in all parts of the country.
When this matter was taken up by the government in 1922 everybody knew-in fact the Prime Minister himself made the statement-that the railway commission and the boards which were operating the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National railways were waiting to see what action the government was going to take in regard1 to the Crowsnest pass agreement before reducing rates on the railways. They were waiting as far back as 1922. I say that the railway commission has not been treated fairly in that the government have not been honest with them, have not let them know what their policy was with regard to the Crowsnest pass agreement until this late day. Early in the present session we had a decision given by the Supreme court with regard to the validity of the act, which was found to apply to certain sections of the country and not to others. It was shown to have been a piece of freak legislation at the outset, and it is entirely inapplicable to conditions in this country today. We may well feel anxious as to the future of our country. We have had during the present session, which is considered by some to be the last session of this parliament, all the evidences of a government that had absolutely no regard for the financial situation which confronts the country. Political expediency apparently is the impelling influence back of the government, they are evidently now trying to make an arrangement with the Progressive group to my left to secure their support. My hon. friends to my left are protesting that they are not getting enough in this measure; they want also to have a cheaper rate on goods shipped from the east, into	the prairie provinces as well as
on commodities going out.	That is
the only thing that will satisfy them. It is only a few weeks ago that they insisted upon the completion of the Hudson Bay railway, and' yet they are complaining about the duplication of railways in western Canada. Well, duplication is not confined to western Canada. We have the same thing in Ontario and in other parts of the country. The old Intercolonial has even been duplicated by the Transcontinental. It was absolutely unfair to the people and uncalled for, but because of the extravagance of the government during

Railway Freight Rates
the early part of this century we have now to pay the penalty for all this duplication, and that is the main reason why it is impossible to get people to go on the land and continue on the land in this country.
It is all very well to say, give the board that is administering the Canadian National railways, a free hand, and allow them to carry on just as they see fit, regardless of the deficits that may result in the operation of the railway; so long as the people of this country will come forward and make up the deficit, in connection with operation, that is what is being done. We are going backwards. We are slipping back at the rate of about $100,000,000 a year in our operation of government railways, and where we are going to land is quite apparent to anyone who has watched the proceedings of this parliament during the present session.	I consider the conduct of the
government in providing for lavish expenditures during the present session, nothing	more or less	than a crime
against the country. And while this is going on there are people in this country by the hundreds, yes by the thousands, who are packing their bags and looking to some other country in which to make a home. It is a serious matter to these people when they have to abandon the country in which they were born, and in which all their interests have been centred during a lifetime. These are the conditions with which we are confronted at this time. What are we doing to meet them?
On this question of railway freight rates the government have dilly-dallied from the outset. The Prime Minister admitted when that committee was appointed, in 1922 5 p.m. that the government was holding up this question of the adjustment of rates until they saw what the findings of that committee would be, and now here we are in the last days of this session in 1925 considering this question. As far as the convenience of the members of this House is concerned, I do not think it matters much whether we get through here in a few days or have to stay here the whole year, now that we have made such a bungle of the country's business. But the government are responsible, and they cannot evade the responsibility. They cannot place it upon this House. The government must accept the responsibility for crippling the railway commission, for interjecting this disturbing element into the railway rate situation in this country. The government must accept the responsibility, and the sooner the people have to decide this 285
matter between the government and themselves the better it will be for all concerned.
I had no desire to participate in this debate, but I have taken the stand from the very outset when this matter was up three years ago that the government should deal with it, and not pretend that they were having a committee of the House appointed to deal with it. In the Speech from the Throne at the opening of this session the question of railway rates and the question of ocean freight rates were two of the chief features dealt with as they also were of the debate on the Address, yet the government sat here day after day during that debate, dumb as oysters, and they would not declare what the government policy was with regard to these questions which had been featured in the Speech from the Throne. We now know the reason why. It was because they wished to bring in this matter at the tail-end of the session in the form of a bill such as we have before us to-day with the hope of getting it through. I believe the predominating influence with this government has been none other than political expediency, bargaining and bartering with certain influences in this country rather than carrying out the view which I am sure the Minister of Railways must entertain with regard to the question.
I do not intend to say anything further with regard to the matter. I am absolutely opposed to this legislation, which interferes with the railway board, which ought to be enabled to deal with the question of railway rates in this country, and also with an adjustment of the scale of wages paid to the employees of the railways, and other privileges extended to them under the awards which have gone into effect in years gone by, with an absolutely free hand.

The hon. gentleman
read certain statements, one from the late chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners and another from the ex-Minister of Railways, casting certain reflections with reference to the wages paid to railway employees. May I ask if the hon. member is not aware that since 1920 the railway employees have contributed to the Dominion of Canada $45,000,000 per year in reductions in wages?
I do not know what my hon. friend means when he says they have contributed $45,000,000 to the Dominion of Canada.

That is the admitted reduction in wages.

Railway Freight Rates

Undoubtedly there
have been some reductions made, but there is in effect to-day a scale or classification in regard to wages, and as to time, that I think is sadly in need of adjustment. I quoted statements made by the chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners at that time. I could give further statements, if I thought it would be of any interest. I might point out that there has been an evident attempt on the part of interested parties to make the railway question a political question. I have before me the main editorial in the Toronto Globe of December 12, 1921, which says:
There were cries of "treachery" when the two leading Conservative papers of Montreal, a few days before the polls opened, ceased to support and began to criticize the Meighen government.
Further on I find the following:
In effect, putting the matter bluntly, the Montreal Star and Gazette, and the powerful group of financiers for which they speak, ceased to help their friends of the Conservative party because Mr. Meighen and his supporters stood to their guns on the question of public ownership and operation of the National Railways.
I am not going to refer to any more editorials, further than to point out that there are certain influences in this country which are determined to have their own way regardless of the general effect on the whole country, and to my mind the only possible way we can deal with this matter is to have a railway commission who are competent, who will exercise their judgment to the best of their ability and who will deal with this matter free of influence from the government or any other source. They must deal with this matter. They are the only people who can deal with it. We have interested parties who are continually using their influence to promote their own ends. We see the result in the stagnation of business. We find our country so badly crippled to-day that we are doubtful as to the future. This matter should be in the hands oif the Board of Railway Commissioners, and consequently I am absolutely opposed to the bill.

I asked the Prime Minister, when he made his statement this morning, a very short question of 'considerable importance to British Columbia. He did not cover it in his statement, and I have written out the question. The Prime Minister referred to the policy of acquisition, and created the impression that it was a policy extending to British Columbia in which we are vitally interested, and I desire to get an answer to my question, which is as follows:
Will the government say now as its definite policy that if British Columbia appealed to the Governor in Council from an adverse ruling of the Board of Rail-

way Commissioners, the government would set aside any ruling of the board which would increase the rates to Vancouver beyond the present rate of 22J cents?
Would the Governor in Council on appeal, so far as the government policy is concerned, fix the rate on grain moving from the prairie provinces to Pacific coast ports at a rate equal to the present Crowsnest rate on grain going eastward so that the present 22i cent rate from Calgary would become 18 cents?
On the word of the Prime Minister favouring equalization, I do not see how the government could honourably refuse to do so. Does the Prime Minister not think British Columbia is entitled to that definite assurance by the government now?

If my hon. friend is not accustomed to the proper reply to give to a hypothetical question, I will say to him that I should not wish at this moment to answer it. If an appeal were made to the Governor in Council on any matter it would be dealt with in accordance with what I have said to-day with regard to the government's policy.

The section as proposed to be amended by Hon. Mr. Graham would read as follows:
But such rates shall apply to all such traffic moving from all points on all lines of railway west of Fort William to Fort William or Port Arthur, over all lines of railway now or hereafter constructed by any company subject to the jurisdiction of parliament.

speechtext: The second amendment is to insert, afteT the word "thereto," in the sixth line, in order to follow the amendment in paragraph 3, the words "within the territory."
Amendment agreed to.

Before we -pass to section
4, I wish to move an amendment, to add a new subsection t*o section 3. I beg to move:
That section 3 be amended by adding as subsection 7 the following:
"In any rates or tariff of rates fixed or approved by the board, rates in the territory lying west of Fort Wiliam in the province of Ontario, and east of the Rocky mountains, shall not exceed by more than ten per cent the rates or tariff of rates fixed or approved for the same commodities in the territory lying east of Sudbury in the province of Ontario, but nothing herein contained shall 'be taken to imply that rates in one territory are to be higher than rates in any other territory."
In order to give the committee the reasons that have induced me to move this amendment, it is necessary to traverse the history of the Crowsnest agreement, and I shaT do

Railway Freight Rates
so as briefly as possible. This Crowsnest pass agreement, as every member of the committee is aware, was placed on the statute books of Canada in 1897. It remained there undisturbed until conditions produced by the war made necessary a suspension of the application of the rates under that agreement, and I am free to say, sir-and I think I am well within the judgment of every member of the committee-that if the war had not occurred, we would have had no discussion as far as abrogation of the Crowsnest agreement and its application to western rates is concerned. The agreement was in the nature of a contract made with the Canadian Pacific Railway. A good deal has been heard in the discussion whcih has taken place in the chamber in the last few days upon the sanctity of contracts. I do not wish to deal with that phase of the question at any length.
I may, however, be permitted to observe that when the Canadian Pacific Railway was issued a charter in 18S1, it had a definite contract, for instance, with the Canadian government, and the Canadian people through the government, in respect of the matter of taxation, and that contract was consistently lived up to by the Canadian people, although in western Canada it imposed serious hardships and burdens upon many sections of the community. I do not wish, however* .to argue on the matter of the contract. The purpose of the contract was not alone to give a subsidy for the building of the Crowsnest pass railway. That 'opportunity whs taken by the government of the day to establish a principle in respect of western rates. The reason for the establishment of that principle is clearly evident. The whole question of freight rates in Canada is complicated and made difficult by the geographical character of the country. We have really in Canada, in the main, two separate communities. We have an eastern community, the eastern section of the country that lies east of the Great Lakes, and the western section of Canada lying west of those Great Lakes. Separating the two is a thousand miles of wilderness which, as I have stated before ton other occasions, is the most significant political fact in Canada to-day. I may interject here that, in my judgment, the greatest task of statesmanship in Canada at this time is to reconcile the diverging interests of those two sections of our country.
The principle that was sought to be established when the Crowsnest pass agreement was given effect to was to afford a measure of protection to western Canada in the matter 285i
of freight rates. In eastern Canada freight rates are governed by water competition. They are at times governed by American rail competition. An instance of this is the grain rates from bay ports to Montreal and St. John. These rates naturally are influenced by the corresponding rates from Buffalo to ports like Philadelphia and New York. Consequently, American rail competition does, within certain limits, affect Canadian eastern rates. But the big factor governing railway rates in eastern Canada, as I stated a moment ago, is water competition. That fact is not denied, and it has not been denied in this debate. In fact, it was admitted in judgments of the railway commission several years ago, particularly in the case that, if my memory serves me aright, was known as the Eastern Rates case. What does this mean? It means a definite limitation on the rail rates that may be established in eastern Canada. That fact, let me repeat for the information of the committee, has governed the railway commission at all times in its consideration of rates.
With that fact I want the committee to couple the next fact which is this. It has been admitted, and it has not been challenged so far in this debate, that the railways must be permitted rates that will enable them to operate. No one will quarrel with that assertion. I may say however, in passing, that even that statement requires some qualification. It requires qualification in this respect, that the country cannot afford to establish rates that will give the railways the necessary returns unless those railways are efficiently and economically managed. Consequently, the factor of economy and efficiency in management enters into the consideration of the question. But, by and large, the position has been taken by successive chairmen of the Board of Railway Commissioners and indeed, by the commission throughout in dts various hearings, and it has been generally recognized amongst the public and not been questioned, that the railways must be permitted rates that will enable them to function and that will give them a reasonable return on their investment.
Hitherto, in all the rate -cases that have been heard in Canada in the last twenty-five years, and particularly in the last ten years, the Canadian Pacific railway has been taken as the basis upon which rates should be fixed, for a very good reason. Everyone recognizes that if rates were established on a basis to enable the Canadian National Railways, ox the various railways that enter into the Can-
Railway Freight Rates

adian 'National railway system to pay all their operating costs and to look after their fixed charges, those rates would have ito be made very much higher than they are to-day, and such rates would enable the Canadian Pacific to earn far and away beyond what it is justly entitled to earn. Therefore, the Canadian Pacific has been taken as the basis for the establishment of rates. Right here., I wish to dissent from the argument advanced in this discussion iby some members oif the committee that it is necessary to establish rates to enable the Canadian National Railways to pay. The argument has been advanced that rates must be established to reduce the deficits on the Canadian National Railways. I submit that on the present capitalisation, of the Canadian National Railways, that cannot be done; that is to say, rates cannot foe established for the National Railways to-day, that will enable it to pay operating costs and fixed 'charges as well. That argument is not a sound argument, and it 'has never been recognized as a sound position .by the railway commission in any cases that have been heard before them.
What then is the bearing of all this on western Canada? The prairie provinces have no natural .competition in rates. I have pointed out to the committee the competition .that exists and the control exercised over rates in eastern Canada by virtue of water competition. There is no water competition in western Canada. Consequently, rates in western Canada from the very day western Canada was opened up, have been higher and, in many cases, much higher than they have been in eastern Canada, and they are much higher -to-day. The Crowsnest pass agreement specifies rates on certain commodities westbound. If you take those rates to-day on all those commodities, even t'he Crowsnest pass rates, they are higher in almost all similar instances than rates in eastern Canada. Is allowance made there for the charges in the east in connection with the empty car collections?

No allowance is made for that. In 1924 the mileage operated in the east was somewhat greater, 4,896 miles, while in the west it was also greater, 8,465. The earnings per mile in the east in that year were $16,632 per mile and in the west $11,312. The expenses per mile in the east were $13,197 and in the west $8,085. Hon. gentlemen will remember that I told them when we were first discussing the matter, that we always had lower expenses in the west, and this demonstrates the truth of that statement. When you speak of the west
you include British 'Columbia?

Yes, that is
right. Now, my hon. friend (Mr. Crerar) is not to blame for the figures he presented to the House; counsel in that particular case had his own axe to grind and he prepared a particular statement which means very little. I was perfectly fair in pointing out that if my hon. friend really believes in his own figures he does not need any Crowsnest pass agreement at all. Rates that are remunerative cannot be raised because that would be unfair and unjust. But there is not a single western
Railway Freight Rates

member in the House who does not know that the Canadian wheat and flour rates are the lowest in the world.
Is not the hon. gentleman aware that the rate on the Canadian Pacific Railway from Goderich to Maritime ports is considerably lower than the Crows-nest rate?

I do not know
that at all; I do know that so far as rates are concerned, the rate per ton per mile in the west is considerably lower than any I know of. If my hon. friend is able to find any considerable tonnage that moves in eastern territory at lower rates then he will quarrel seriously with the rate per ton figures showing the actual results as I have given them to the committee already, as being in eastern territory 1.173 as against .87 in western territory. All hon. members to my left who are members of the Railway committee know how the accounts are kept in the Canadian National and they know what the results are. If there is any truth whatever in this range of figures, why is it that the territory, the east, which it is said has such low rates is carrying the territory that has the high rates? The heavy tonnage was in the west all right. If there is the slightest economic truth behind the figures used by my hon. friend from Marquette why is it that in a year when central Canada produces a surplus of $22,000,000, the territory where we are told the rates are so high and the tonnage so great shows a loss of $2,200,000?
You refer to the whole western territory right through to Prince Rupert, I suppose?
Certainly.
Is it fair to do so?

I would have
thought so. Why not? We are told the rates are even more out of line in British Columbia. It is all very well for hon. gentlemen to my left to say, "We have to carry the Grand Trunk Pacific to Prince Rupert." But we have to carry the same sort of stuff in the " long bridge " and the Transcontinental. Do not think you have any monopoly of these burdens. In that western territory where, according to my hon. friend (Mr. Crerar), the rates are so high and the tonnage so great, in that particular year there is a deficit in connection with the National Railways of $2,200,000, while in central Canada we produced a surplus of $22,000,000. Mr. Chairman, the thing is ridiculous. And, what is more, it is entirely against the in-
terest of that western territoiy that such statements should be made. The worst thing that can happen to the western territory is to have its 80 per cent of traffic treated in the same way that it is treated in eastern Canada. Just see the fairness of this loaded proposition. Special rates for the heavy movement of western Canada; no! special rate for the heavy movement of central Canada They are to have their special privileges, but in so far as the rates are concerned where the tonnage is heavy in central Canada, where there are commodity rates, notwithstanding the fact that they are not much interested in that business and very little moves under it, they are to come within 10 per cent of the same basis.
Are these grain rates high? Very profitable? Just let us see, Mr. Chairman. I made reference to the application by the railway carriers in United States grain territory on the prairies to the south for an increase in rates. I want the House to realize what rates these railways seek to have so substantially increased. First let us take the short distances. For 420 miles out of Fort William the rates in Canada are 14 cents per hundred pounds; for 417 miles in the American territory they are 204 cents. Portage la Prairie with its mileage of 475 has a rate of 15 cents; a similar mileage in American territory has a rate of 23 cents. Carberry with its mileage of 525 has a rate of 16 cents; for the comparative mileage in United States territory the rate is 234 cents. I take these small mileages because the density of movement in the shorter hauls is greater in the States than it is with us. If we take the longer mileages in which we are so much interested, we find the Lethbridge rate is 25 cents, as against 48 cents for a similar mileage in the United States. That is the class of rates that these companies are seeking to have increased. Let us take another feature of rate structures. The average .rate in western territory was .87 cents on all traffic carried by the Canadian Pacific. The American companies are appealing to the Interstate Commerce Commission because they say they cannot get along with an average per ton revenue as high as 12.09 mills. Why, in 1921, one of their lean years, their revenue was 14.22 mills-nearly 14 cents-as against .87 cents. Yet they are saying they cannot get along with that revenue. Why? Because it is impossible to borrow money, their earnings being insufficient to attract investors. They are quarrelling with earnings which yield them a trifle under 4 per cent on their investment. They want to get

Railway Freight Rates
5| per cent on the actual cash investment in their property. Here, as I pointed out the other day, we have the Canadian Pacific on the actual cash invested in their property earning a little over 4.3 or 4.4 per cent. I am pointing out, Mr. Chairman, that this is a pretty good confirmation of the figures of the National Railways.
Now, I should like hon. gentlemen to my left to again consider this grain business. I gave an illustration the other day as to how quickly things can change in this connection. The statistics worked out by the statistical department which I gave to the House are much more refined than what I am now going to give, they are more correct because they eliminate charges which, in part, cannot fairly be charged to the grain movement less yardage and the like; those are deducted in connection with the five and six million dollar odd loss I gave to the House. I should like hon. gentlemen to do a little figuring on this themselves, and as apparently they did not quite understand them I want to give the figures again. These figures nearly approximate what we are doing ourselves on the National system. Take a total freight traffic of seven billion ton miles, with an average rate per ton per mile of .55 cents. Let us assume that the grain traffic is 60 per cent of that, and in round numbers let us take it again, as I took it the other day, at four billion ton miles. Now, we have an average rate on our grain of .52 cents. Let us assume an operating ratio of 70 per cent. Then the average cost per ton mile is 70 multiplied by 55 divided by 100; that gives your average rate per ton per mile. Your operating ratio1 is 70 per cent of those receipts, that would give you for your cost .385 cents per ton mile. I think that is clear because there is no hing of an Einstein character about this at all. It is perfectly clear to everybody who wants to understand it and who really ought to understand it. That would give a net operating profit on grain of .52 cents which is the grain rate, less the .385 cents which is the average cost per ton mile, yielding a profit of . 135 cents per ton mile. Now hon. gentlemen might think that was a very small thing, but it is a big thing. That was one of the reasons why I have always attributed much more money to this business than many railroaders did. That little decimal .135 of but one cent on a traffic of 4.000.000,000 ton miles gives a profit of $5,400,000. Now, just see how easy that is changed? Supposing we take the figures which we 'had last year, the same 7,000.000.000 ton miles of traffic with an average rate per ton mile of .763 cents.
The general average rate has been raised, But we will take the round figures for the grain traffic of sixty per cent at 4,000.000,000 miles. The grain rate did not go up with the others; the grain rate still stands at .52 cents although the average goes up to .763 cents. Now, supposing we take the operating ratio which obtained, that is 91.08 per cent, make the same calculation and you have a cost per ton mile of .694 cents, resulting in an operating loss of the difference between that cost .694 and .52 cents or .172 cents, bringing about an actual loss of $6,880,000.
I do not think I should further delay the committee except to point out that my hon. friend wants the same rates as in the east. We would welcome that if it were not for one thing-we want to see the west function. My hon. friend wants the same paper rates as in the east, which will not help anybody except some newspaper editors, or some politician who wants to create a grievance here and a grievance there. I would have no objeotion if it were not for one thing. That is we all want to see the west continue to grow and prosper. If that is what my hon. friend wants let us in all fairness refer the whole matter, without any limitation, to the railway board. If it is my hon. friend's wish he can have the whole matter referred therej_ but it will not do to try and load the dice in two directions at the same time.

I am not going to delay
the committee more than a minute or two. My chief utterance will be that the government cannot accept this amendment, for the simple reason that if an amendment is to be accepted to give special treatment to a particular territory, even in addition to the special treatment in the extended territories covered by the Crowsnest pass agreement, on grain and flour, then let us throw the matter wide open and give the same treatment to all parts of Canada. The government has endeavoured, and hon. members have shown on all sides a wish, to meet the desires of the west, but our kind-heartedness does not. seem to have 'been appreciated. If this additional advantage is to be given to the prairies extending to the Rocky mountains, then I say ignore the Rocky mountains and go through to British Columbia. If this additional advantage is going to be given to the prairies then open it up to the province of Ontario, give it to Quebec, give it to the Maritime provinces, and allow your railways to go to the demnition 'bow-wows.

The minister had better go right on now and deal with the whole problem.
Railway Freight Rates

Well, as I pointed out in the House before, we are endeavouring to meet the views of a part of Canada that has had the Orowsnest pass rate for a long time. We are endeavouring to meet that situation, not so much for the people themselves as to meet the psychology of the situation so that the people of the prairie provinces will have no opportunity to feel that they have not been treated generously, I would say, in comparison with the other parts of Canada. I think I need not make any further explanation, I think my hon. friends will see that the government and parliament could not accept that amendment to give still further preferential treatment to the prairies over every other part of Canada.

I will not detain the committee for any length of time except to say a word or two in support of the amendment which I think to be a very generous one from the standpoint of western Canada. The government in putting forward their proposition made two or three claims with which I want to deal. In the first place they claimed they were delivering the country from the confusion in which it found itself at the present time with regard to freight rates. I want to ask who produced the confusion, and why? One of the parties to the agreement is responsible for producing the confusion, and the reason for producing confusion was to defeat the declared will of parliament, to dispossess the west., and to fool the people of Canada. That is why confusion was produced, one of the most astounding pieces of psychological trickery this country has known. It reminds me of the trick of the pickpocket who will cause a disturbance in a crowd in order that his colleagues may get away with the jewelry. That was the cause of this confusion that has been projected into the minds of the people of Canada. This is the very thing that inspired Aesop's fable about the wolf and the lamb. You remember how the wolf stirred up the mud in the stream in order to have an excuse to devour the lamb. The railways of this country have precipitated the situation which is poisoning the mind of Canada, and if the public mind had not been poisoned the government could not have got away with this bill to-night. Now, the government by their passive attitude were responsible for allowing that poison to work in the public mind. A psychological situation has been created by the supineness of the government. They are responsible for it indirectly, and yet to-day they are bragging because this bill is going to cure the situation 
that they themselves helped to create. It is like a physician exposing a man to contagion, and then bragging because he has helped to cure him. That is the situation the government are in. Since last July they have condoned the action of the railways, one of the parties concerned in the agreement, in poisoning the public mind of Canada, and to-night they are taking advantage of that state of public mind. I challenge the government to say whether they could have got away with this if the ground had not been very carefully prepared for them.

May I answer that question? If the government did not stand as the buffer, the whole Crowsnest agreement would have been wiped out at this session by an enormous majority. The government has been trying to protect my hon. friend so far as it could, and now it gets abuse for doing so.

Why would the Crowsnest
pass agreement have been wiped out at this session? Because the public mind of Canada had been prepared for wiping it out, and the government has been a party to that.

We can do it yet if you
go too strong.

The real situation this last
few days has not been the confused state of the freight rates in Canada; it has been the confused state of the public mind into which the freight rate situation has brought it. During this debate the government has not been free from the attempt to put upon us the onus, as though we were trying to defend an indefensible position, a position that is bringing Canada into a state of utter confusion in regard to- its freight rates. The thing to be discriminated in the public mind -it may be too late-but what we want to discriminate in our minds is between the Crowsnest pass agreement as it stands tonight and as it will stand until this bill is carried, and the Crowsnest pass agreement as we knew it prior to 1917. We are not standing for the Crowsnest pass agreement as it stands to-night; we want the Crowsnest pass agreement as it stood prior to 1917.
The CHAIRMAN; I would call the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that this debate has been limited by the amendment that has been moved by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar). There is another general clause of the bill dealing with rates.

If I get my remarks over all
at once, Mr. Chairman, it will relieve me of the necessity of speaking later.

Get it all out and you
will feel better.

The Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) in presenting his case said that there were only three alternatives-to destroy the Crowsnest pass agreement, to continue it as it is, or to accept his own intermediary proposition. Now we on this side do not admit that there are only three alternatives. There was another alternative, and that was to restore the Crowsnest pass agreement as we understood it prior to 1917, and I might say, after listening to the case of the Solicitor General, prior to the decision of the Supreme court itself, because even the government itself according to his generous interpretation, stood for the old Crowsnest pass agreement until that date.
The Minister of Railways said that this bill was necessary in order to save the railways. He might as well have said that at first. I believe that that is the motive of 9 p.m. the whole bill, to save the railways. These are the words he used. He said: " Parliament can ruin the railways." Now I think that is the gist of his whole position. Parliament can ruin the railways. The attitude we take expresses itself oppositely from that. We believe that the railways can ruin the people whom parliament is supposed to represent, and we believe that the railways will ruin the people if they do not wake up. We have abundant evidence to show that it is the people who need protection against the railways. We have come to the point, as one writer says, where we no longer ride on the railways, but the railways ride upon us, and they would ride upon us still more if the people themselves did not have some degree of say in this House. Parliament can ruin the railways indeed but this parliament, as it is presently constituted, has not much chance of ruining the railways. The railways have too many stout defenders in this House for parliament ever to ruin them. We have listened to some extremely good briefs during this debate on behalf of the railways. We have not heard any similar brief on behalf of the people of western Canada. We have had one or two good speeches on behalf of the west, but we have had nothing equal to some of the lawyerlike statements made on behalf of the railways in this debate. No, Mr. Chairman, there is not much chance of this parliament ruining the railways if it continues to be constituted as it is at the present time. The Crowsnest pass agreement, when it was first instituted, was meant to safeguard the people.

I am sorry. I will endeavour
to shape my remarks to meet with your views, Mr. Chairman. I was proceeding to say that the Crowsnest pass agreement in its first intention was meant to safeguard the rights of the people. That is the distinction between the original agreement and this bill. This bill is framed to safeguard the railways. The original agreement that we are asked to give up for this was meant to safeguard the people. That is the distinction between the old and the new, and that is the way it will work out so far as I can see.
The Minister of Railways complained that the yardstick, as he called it, as laid down by the Crowsnest pass agreement, was too short for modern conditions. He gave no proof of it, and I do not think there is any proof of it. I think the hon. member for Marquette proved conclusively that the yardstick laid down by the Crowsnest pass agreement is abundantly long enough even for present conditions. But supposing it was not long enough, supposing the yardstick had shrunk relatively, supposing it was no longer adapted; is the proposition of this bill before us the right one? This is to do away with the yardstick altogether. Is that the right proposition? I believe that the amendment is the right one, because it introduces what this bill alone abolishes; it reintroduces the yardstick, as the minister calls it. It lays down a standard by which rates in western Canada as they have been in the past will be determined in relation to rates in the east, where special factors enter into the situation, and will guarantee to western shippers a measure of justice.

Would the hon.
gentleman be agreeable to laying down the yardstick for other parts of the Dominion?

I think what I have just said
implied that a yardstick was necessary for the west in the sense that it was necessary for the east, because the east, as has been said over and over again in this debate, has its

controlling factors, not only in the water competition but in the American railways. We regret that these extraordinary pecautions should be necessary, but we .cannot help the situation in which we find ourselves and if the Crowsnest pass agreement with its yardstick was necessary twenty-five years ago, it is necessary now. That is one thing that no person has dealt with in this debate. There was a reason for the institution of the Crowsnest pass agreement and that reason was the exposed position of the western shipper as compared with the eastern shipper. The Crowsnest pass agreement was not instituted for nothing. It was not a freak. We are not contending for the former rates, but for a principle. It is all very well to say, "Trust the board", as our hon. friends to our right have stated. It is like asking Esau to trust Jacob.

speaker dealt very fully with the question of equalization. The ex-Minister of Finance
did nothing but talk about rates.

I cannot talk about rates
unless I bring in the railway commission. It seems to me to be a new conception of British government that we should relegate the most vital things in matters of government to commissions. Here we have something more important than taxation so far as the west is concerned. No proper conception of the British constitution would tolerate for a moment the relegation of taxation to a commission which had no responsibility to anyone, Which represented nobody; and yet that is what our friends to my right would have us do. speechtext:

It comes badly from hon. gentlemen to the right as well as from our friends opposite to talk about narrow-eyed sectionalism. We always hear that plea put forward, at least we have heard it in the last four years, whenever anything vital to the west has been considered. I say this feelingly, because on all other matters we have heard the same plea; and to-night the Crowsnest agreement is going the way of the Hudson Bay railway. And their going is none the more graceful for the paeans of praise that come from the other side. These two things have gone and their going dates from the same time, 1917,

which was so fatal a year for western Canada. What western Canada has lost in the interval she has not made up and from all appearances to-night there will be no chance of her making it up. I therefore as energetically and earnestly as I can make my protest against the passing of this bill.

The amendment proposes a
restriction on the freedom of action of the railway commission, and the question arises as to why the railway commission should be restricted in any way. Our friends to the right argue that the commission should not be restricted at all, but I think it must be apparent to everyone in this House that there is at least a large section of the Canadian people who have lost confidence in the board. For one reason or another which I do not intend discussing, the Board of Railway Commissioners, on whom I make no reflection, have lost the confidence of a section of the Canadian people; and that being the case it would seem necessary that some kind of restriction should logically be imposed on the board. Even if we all had confidence in the board I think that it is only a fair proposition that some sort of basis of action should be specifically laid down by this House for the board to take; there should be some fixed principle to be applied. I do not see that up to the present time any such principle has been in force. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) has argued, very well I think, that the board ought to be provided with certain principles upon which to act, just as our courts are given laws to interpret and apply. But so far there has been nothing adequate of that kind provided the board. If the Minister of Railways now or sometime in a subsequent parliament would lay down some definite principles of equalization or otherwise for the board to interpret and apply, I do not think we should be in the position we now find ourselves in, and in which we have been for the past few years. I would suggest that until a sufficient body of principles is laid down in our Railway Act in the matter of freight rates it is perfectly logical and necessary, and not at all to be disparaged, that this parliament, representing the people, should tie the hands of the railway board in some way to prevent either discriminatory or, shall I say, unpatriotic action. There is a disposition here to regard as unwarranted any attempt at restricting the action of the board. But I submit that it is perfectly logical and desirable that until such time arrives as we have established certain adequate principles for the board to apply, some restriction of the kind should be adopted, limiting the freedom of action of the board.

The decision has not yet been given, and according to the way in which section 4 is worded, if this amendment is not earned, even suppose the decision of the Privy Council were in favour of the province, they would not be able to reap any benefit from that decision. They would not be able to have the advantage of those rates. All they would be able to get -would be that they would have to pay the bill of expenses. If this amendment is added to this clause and it so turns out that the decision is in favour of the province oi Manitoba, then they will have the advantage for which they have paid in the years gone by. This does not otherwise injure the bill in any way. It is simply a proviso added to this clause of the bill.

The leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) has forsaken the Crowsnest pass agreement, and he is now going to rely upon a Manitoba agreement in place of it.
Mr, FORKE:	You are wiping out the
agreements.

Not at all. So far as the Canadian Northern was concerned in the Manitoba agreement, that was to assist the movement of grain, flour, and so forth. The committee will, I think, realize with me that one of the objects of this bill is to wipe out, not litigation, but a judgment of the Supreme court which was given restricting the territory which comes under the Crowsnest pass agreement to points on the Canadian Pacific line in existence in 1897. The Supreme court on a question submitted to them in connection with the rates question a few weeks ago, decided that that territory was restricted to the limits existing in 1897. In order to protect the western people in what we think are their rights, we are not only interfering with litigation, but wiping out a judgment of the

Railway Freight Rates
Supreme court given only a few weeks ago. By doing that, we are taking away from the railways the right to appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, which appeal they were prepared to make had it not been for this legislation. We are interfering, not only with litigation, but with judgments, and that being the case, I submit that this committee, if this amendment is carried, would really be going back on the whole intent of this bill, which is to straighten out all these difficulties and make plain sailing for an equalization of rates. The question of the Manitoba agreement was brought before the Board of Railway Commissioners and it was decided against that province. An appeal which was made on a matter of law to the Supreme court, was decided against the province of Manitoba in that court. I think I speak advisedly when I say that there are very few legal men in the Dominion of Canada who have any idea that Manitoba can hope to succeed before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
Why take away the opportunity?

Because this legislation is to take out of litigation this whole freight rate question and to place it on a basis where it can be handled by the Board of Railway Commissioners. As the object of the bill is to get rid of litigation and, further, to override a decision of the Supreme court, I am sure hon. gentlemen will not ex-, pect the government to accept an amendment which overrides the whole principle of the bill.

I would ask my hon. friend to reconsider that question, looking at it from this standpoint. I am familiar with the agreement. The matter came before me when I was on the Board of Railway Commissioners, and the application of the agreement was considered by that board. I did not give effect to it, and at that time I believe I gave leave to appeal to the Supreme court. I should like my hon. friend to consider the question in this way which seems to me to be the fair way. We are not parties to that agreement. I do not know that I insist anything we are doing in this legislation is going to change that agreement-
I do not see it does.

-but I think the committee ought to consider carefully whether, in connection with a bill which, on its face, deals merely with difficulties arising under the Crowsnest pass agreement, we
should take away any right which may exist to the province of Manitoba as a result of their own agreements. It might be that if the province got what it wanted, it would .be like the boy that got hold of a bear, but the people of that province do not think so. They think they have a legal right. Our usual practice is not to interfere with rights subject to litigation. This litigation is actually going on, and I would submit to my hon. friend that the litigation might just as well go on and the usual rule be applied, that is that parliament, in its legislation, does not interfere with pending litigation.

I do not see the matter in that way at all. This bill is a bold piece of legislation in order to get rid, not only of the Crowsnest pass agreement, but of a score of agreements of more or less importance. Now, we are asked to pick out one special agreement, which my hon. friend, as chairman of the Board of Railw'ay Commissioners, has ruled against, and as regards which the Supreme court has upheld him in his judgment, and we are asked to suspend that because an appeal has been made to the judicial Committee of the Privy Council. If we do that, then I do not think we . have any right to take away from the railways their right to appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, and we are doing that definitely in this bill. Why not let us get the rate situation cleared away and not surround the Board of Railway Commissioners with any more restrictions than we can avoid? If we do what the hon. member suggests, the case can be dangled before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council for two or three years, and equalization of railway rates in Canada cannot start until that litigation is over.

Does the minister think it
would not be worth fighting for, supposing the Privy Council decided in favour of Manitoba?

I do not think so. I still
maintain that if we do this we are making a great mistake; we are nullifying our whole action of the past three days in trying to get rid of a number of agreements-and we have a number of agreements on the Intercolonial, some of small importance, some of greater importance-in order to give the Board of Railway Commissioners a fair chance. It is not right to allow litigation in one case to go on and by legislation to prevent other litigants from appealing their oase. 1 never dreamed for a moment that any person would take this stand. Otherwise, this legislation would have been framed altogether differently.

Supply-Public Works

Is Wellington street the

I should like to suggest to the minister that he place some police on Wellington street so that it would not be so dangerous to cross there. ' I think it is the most dangerous street to cross in the city of Ottawa. I had the matter brought to my attention by different parties in the city, and from personal experience I would rather cross any other street in Ottawa than Wellington street, We have so many policemen around this building and the grounds here that surely we could have an officer placed on Wellington street in front of the parliament buildings to direct the traffic there and make it safe for people to cross the street without incurring the danger of being run down every time they cross.

I am making

I think that next year we should make a regulation,- I have the matter in mind,-that during the session at least there should be no cars parked in front of the parliament buildings.

I was just going to raise that question. I have gone out very often when there was just room to get between the cars. The driver of a car coming along the street will not see a person coming out of the grounds, and a person coming out of the grounds will not see the cars approaching. It is a very dangerous situation.

Before the item carries I
should like to say that I think we need more protection than has been suggested. I think we need a policeman there to regulate the speed at which these cars go by. There are no cross streets intersecting Wellington street in front of the parliament buildings, and lots of these cars go by at the rate of thirty miles an hour. They pay no respect to the centre line of the street, they take any side at all, and persons crossing Wellington street to get to the parliament buildings really endanger their own lives. I think this government could easily afford to place one of our mounted 
policemen on this street and if necessary stop these cars once in a while in order to enable people to cross in safety.

I will be very
glad to give consideration to what my hon. friend has said.
Either that or have a few trenches dug across .so that the cars would not be able to go so fast.

salaries of engineers, firemen and watchmen in Ottawa,

The Department
of Public Works have a staff who do their purchasing. There is a secretary of the commission who reports to council through the responsible minister, and keeps track of these purchases.

It is done

Yes.

furniture made in the penitentiaries?
I think we have bought some tables and chairs and brooms from the penitentiaries.

I think that question has been under consideration.

I think it has been
suggested from time immemorial that the inmates of the penitentiaries should be given more work, that they should be self-sustaining, that that would help towards defraying the big expenditure on account of the penitentiaries. I think sufficient work should be given to enable the inmates to be kept busy. Furniture making is an occupation that a man can learn pretty quickly. It is not very technical, and I think the government would be well advised to have all the furniture for all the departments made in the penitentiaries.
The Penitentiaries ' branch have an agent who is in and out of the departments all the time, and we do buy a certain amount from the penitentiaries, but not exclusively from them.

The penitentiaries

That is an old
question. It has been discussed many times, but there are difficulties in the way.

Why don't they grow
potatoes and wheat to?

There is nothing to
prevent them growing potatoes, although I might say that the more potatoes they grew within the last year or two, the further they would be in debt. I would rather see them working at something there was money in.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We are
buying more than we used to from the penitentiaries.
I am convinced that it is through pressure from firms who are manufacturing furniture that the government do not buy more furniture from the penitentiaries.

There are some
styles of furniture they can make in the peni-

Supply-Public 'Works
tentiaries, but generally speaking they could not fill many of the requirements of the government.
What percentage of the government's furniture is manufactured in the penitentiaries?

I have not that
information, but I know there has been a tendency in recent years to give more of this work to the penitentiaries.

I think the policy should be pursued of making all these institutions as nearly self-supporting as possible. The hon. gentleman across the way asked, why do these institutions not grow potatoes and wheat.
I can only say they do.
For themselves.

Not only for themselves.
The asylum at Brandon I know has a very expert hog raiser in charge, and he takes car after car of hogs and sells them on the Winnipeg market in competition with the farmers' hogs. I am not objecting to that. Nobody is complaining about it, but when the question is put up to us, why don't they grow potatoes and wheat, I simply say they do. These institutions should all grow as much as possible of the vegetables and the food that they need. I think it is only a matter of sound public policy that that should be done. These institutions are necessary for taking care of various classes in the community, some who are insane, some who are morally derelict and have to be taken under the law, and this is a burden which the country necessarily has to bear, but the support of these institutions should not be made an occasion for furnishing other people with the opportunity to sell their supplies. I think these institutions as much as possible might be used not only to provide for themselves but to provide for the heeds of the government. I know there are objections, but personally I have none to allowing the output of these institutions to be put on the market under fair competition, not cut-throat competition, with the products of free labour. There is no reason why, because men have had to be taken care of by the state they should be deprived of the opportunity of earning something-

How could my hon. friend
establish fair competition in the matter of wages?

By selling at even prices
with the products of free labour. I think we can pursue much further than we have done
the policy of making all these institutions self-supporting.

The fact that the institution called the penitentiary is making supplies for the government is not on a par with a case where an institution is manufacturing for sale in the open market. This is simply one department under government control. It is one of the government institutions and I do not see any good reason why the manufacturer of any article should object to the government having one department under their care manufacturing goods which they need in some of their departments. That is not manufacturing articles to be placed in the open market in competition with the products of other manufacturers. If the goods were to be placed in 'the open market some objection might legitimately be made. I do not think they have a strong case-in fact I do not think they have any case at all- when they object to the penitentiaries manufacturing anything they can produce for the government's own use. That is common sense, sound policy and fair and right to everybody.
I do not think it is fair to the taxpayers to make them pay taxes to maintain an institution that can maintain itself by manufacturing goods needed in some other department of the government.

Item agreed to.
Heating, $420,000.

Does this cover the heating
for all Dominion public buildings?

Yes, outside of
Ottawa.

Could the minister explain
this item to us? I have been looking at the next item, which is heating. The bill for lighting seems to be very excessive.

I think not. This amount is required for the purchase of fuel. It costs more to heat a home or a house than to light it, and I think this is probably just about right. Our coal supplies are bought carefully by tender, and I think the charges are reasonable.

Coal is all bought by

Yes.

If I had any criticism
to offer to the lighting bill, I would say that it was excessive as compared with the cost of heating. I should not imagine it would cost fifty per cent as much to light the

Supply-Public Works

building as to heat it, especially in the cold weather, where you have to heat your buildings all day. In the summer you require very little light, especially when we have daylight saving. We do not need nearly so much light now as in the winter. That is probably one of the excuses in favour of daylight saving.

No.
Does it include janitors?

No, not the
janitors.

What does it include
besides coal?

There were
36,500 tons of coal required and purchased. Wood is also required for various buildings. Then we have the removal of ashes, the supply of heating gas, steam heating and fuel oil.

Does it include the
firemen?

No, it is for the
purchase of fuel of various kinds and the removal of ashes.

Under what head do
