Next item, salaries of caretakers, engineers, firemen and so on.
This item would indicate that it included all the cost of heating. Evidently this does not. This should be called cost of fuel, instead of heating.

Yes, fuel or
neating.

Item agreed to.
Light, $207,000.

This is the item I was drawing the minister's attention to. It seem3 to me this amount is excessive compared to the cost of heating the buildings. Take the buildings in Ottawa; the lighting is less than one-fourth of the amount of the heating. Possibly the minister has some explanation of the high cost of lighting.

How many buildings are
there?

There are four
hundred and sixty-three.

Are they all outside of
Ottawa?
Yes.

It must cost $700 on an
average for each building.

The cost varies
very much.
It seems to me a very excessive charge for lighting.

The trouble with a lot of
public buildings is that they require to have light night and day. The Brandon asylum is a magnificent building in many respects. At one time an expert came over from the United States to inspect the buildings up there, and he found this building was quite adequate in every way, except in regard to lighting. He said the building should not have required as much electric lighting as it was found necessary to consume there. In a great many corridors they burn the light twenty-four hours a day.

That is true in
most of the city buildings.

I am no architect, but it
seems to me the great weakness in many public buildings is that they are not adequately lighted from the outside.
I would suggest that in many cases they pull up the blinds and let in the light.

Is the light supplied by meter?

Supply-Public Works
Yes.
Is there anyone who supervises the buildings and sees that the lights are turned out in the day time?
Oh yes.

I have seen the lights burning
in the parliament buildings all day.
Not all day.

For very many hours in the
morning, in broad daylight, the lights are burning. Of course the minister is not to blame for that.

I noticed it the
other morning myself. The same complaint was brought to my attention early in the session, but they tell me that at certain times of the day the electrician, in charge of what they call the white way makes his test, turns on the lights and goes over the circuit. They do the same thing in other places.

I do not think anything should be done in the matter of placing them except with the approval of the donor. There are many

I am thankful for the
way in which the minister has received the suggestion. In this connection I desire to make a brief statement as to the history of these paintings. I do not think that the fact is as well appreciated as it should be that these paintings now in the possession of this Dominion are due first of all to the resourceful
initiative, the intense ardour for this country, and the generosity of Lord Beaverbrook. Lord Beaverbrook, as we all know, is a Canadian not only by birth but in heart as well; and though I cannot claim any friendship or, indeed, any intimacy with him whatever, I do feel that we owe him a great debt of gratitude for the thoughtfulness he displayed in preserving the records of the war in various forms to be the property and the pride of this Dominion for years to come.
The conflict had not much more than started when he conceived the idea of seeing that an adequate record was kept 'of the activities and the achievements of the Canadian forces in the field; and with characteristic initiative he set about to make himself responsible that this should be done. The eyewitness service owed its origin to him solely, and that service, distinct as it was from the rather dry and formal official records, is today the material, very complete, vivid and reliable, from which the history of the war is being written so far as Canada is concerned. The initial organization was expanded until it embraced all the Canadian units, and it certainly- is not too much to say that no army in the field of all the allied armies was so served in this respect as was Canada.
But what I rose to mention chiefly was the gift- of these paintings. They are considered the best of any of the paintings of the war and I understand that they are of a value approximating one million dollars, and possibly much more than that. Undoubtedly in the future they will be of far greater value. The idea and the execution of it are solely Lord Beaverbrook's. From beginning to end it was simply a work for Canada, and I regret exceedingly that in our time as in the time since its value has not been adequately recognized, nor have the pictures themselves been so placed and used as to give the Canadian people the results which Lord Beaverbrook had a right to expect they would receive. I know that owing to their character there must be a building suited for their display, and I 'earnestly trust that we shall be in a position soon to provide that building for the practical *purposes of demonstration to show to the people of Canada the records of the war in this particular form. I attribute some laxity7 in this respect to the late government. I sincerely hope, however, that in this regard the 'present administration will far excel what we did in relation to these pictures. I make reference to the subject only because I believe that the Canadian people should not lose sight of the real service that was rendered this country by one of her sons, and that he
Sup-ply-Public Works

Item agreed to.
Grant to the Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company towards construction of bridge over the second narrows of Burrard inlet, B.C. being revote of portion of subsidy authorized by statute, chap. 46, sec. 3, 1913. Revote-$100,000-$270,000.

Would the minister explain
why he is going to contribute to the cost of this bridge and give us some information about the proposed expenditure?

This is for the
construction of a bridge across the second narrows of Burrard inlet. In 1913, I think, parliament made a grant, under the Railway Act, 
of some $350,000 to a private enterprise to assist in the construction of this bridge. That project did not succeed. Later on the municipalities of Vancouver city, North Vancouver city, and the district of North Vancouver and West Vancouver organized themselves into what is known as the Burrard National Tunnel and Bridge Company and have subscribed to this undertaking. They properly, I think, came to the Dominion government and asked if we would assist in the construction of this bridge. We at that time, in 1922, voted $100,000. That vote was repeated in 1924. The province of British Columbia also contributed $120,000 to this undertaking. So it is a municipal, provincial and Dominion government undertaking. When I was west last summer, I was met by a large delegation of men using the channel for the towing of logs and the running of their boats in various lines of trade, and they complained of the fact that a cheap kind of bridge was 'being built, that it was obstructing the natural outlet through the narrows and would cause adverse currents to navigation. The matter seemed to be of a more or less serious nature, and as the undertaking was one in which the smaller municipalities were involved to the extent of their credit, I thought it wise that the matter should be cleared up rather than have the undertaking gone on with and cause probably some damage to the passage way that we require at certain sections of the bridge, and thus lead to a difficult situation. I had a board of engineers go into the whole matter, and they reported that to relieve and improve conditions there should be a further expenditure of $170,000, which would provide for the adding of two spans, 150 feet, north of pier No. 1; to raise the existing piers five feet and approaches, $78,000; dredging, $88,000; and diversion at Seymour creek $33,000. These matters were all taken into consideration and I asked council that we place in the estimates this year $270,000 for this undertaking. .The bridge is an important one. It will give the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific access to the north shore of Burrard inlet, and will permit of industrial and other development on that shore, giving them the advantage of railway traffic. It will also accommodate pedestrian and vehicular traffic in and out of Vancouver and on to the north shore. The bridge is an important one, as I have already said, and has been endorsed by this parliament to the extent of a grant of SIOO.OOO, and by previous parliaments to the extent of $350,000, when it was a private undertaking.
